title: Never move a tag that has been published
summary: You tagged the wrong commit and pushed. Moving the tag is possible, and it quietly leaves every colleague pointing at different code under the same name. See it happen, then do it properly.
mental_model: A tag is a promise that a name always means one commit. Moving it breaks that promise silently: clones keep the old target and nothing warns anybody, because git never overwrites an existing tag on fetch.
danger: Retagging is one of the few git operations with no local signal that anything is wrong. Two machines can build 'v2.0.0' and get different binaries.

commit.message: Fix the bug that shipped in 2.0.0

steps.title: See what everyone currently agrees on
steps.why: You, the server and your colleague all have v2.0.0 pointing at the buggy commit. That agreement is the only thing that makes a tag useful.

steps.title: Move the tag onto the fix
steps.why: `-f` overwrites the tag locally. It feels like the obvious fix: the release should have included the bug fix, so point the name at the fixed commit.
steps.expect: The tag now points at the newer commit.

verify.label: the tag now points at the fixed commit
verify.hint: git tag -f -a v2.0.0 -m "..." (note: rev-parse on an annotated tag gives the tag object's sha, not the commit's — use v2.0.0^{} for that)

steps.title: Publishing it needs force too
steps.why: The server refuses a normal push of an existing tag — that refusal is git protecting the promise. Forcing overrides it.

steps.title: Now look at the colleague's clone
steps.why: Here is the damage. They fetch, git sees they already have a tag called v2.0.0, and leaves it alone. They are still on the buggy commit and nothing tells them.
steps.expect: BROKEN = True — the old code, under the new release name.

verify.label: the colleague's v2.0.0 still points at the buggy commit

steps.title: The only way they find out
steps.why: `--force` on fetch, or `--prune-tags`, overwrites local tags. Nobody runs these by habit — which is exactly why retagging is unsafe rather than merely inconvenient.
steps.expect: Now they get the fixed commit — but only because they knew to force.

verify.label: a forced fetch finally updated their tag

steps.title: Do it the honest way instead
steps.why: Cut a new version. v2.0.1 is unambiguous, every clone gets it with a normal fetch, and the history of what shipped when stays true.
commands: git tag -a v2.0.1 -m "Release 2.0.1 — fixes the 2.0.0 bug"

verify.label: a new patch release was published instead
verify.hint: git tag -a v2.0.1 && git push origin v2.0.1

steps.title: Confirm the patch release needs no force anywhere
steps.why: The colleague fetches normally and gets v2.0.1, because the name is new. No force, no coordination, no chance of two machines disagreeing.

verify.label: the new tag arrived with an ordinary fetch
the fix shipped as a new patch release
verify.hint: cut v2.0.1 rather than relying on the retag

verify.label: the colleague received it with a plain fetch
and it contains the fixed code

pitfalls: `git fetch --tags` does NOT update a tag that already exists locally. Moving a published tag therefore fails silently for everyone who already had it.
Docker images, package registries and CI caches keyed on a tag name will keep serving the old artefact after a retag.
If you truly must retag, tell everyone to run `git fetch --tags --force` — and expect several of them not to.
Deleting and recreating a tag is the same operation with the same consequences. The problem is the name reuse, not the flag.
cheatsheet: move a tag locally — think first
the only way clones pick up a moved tag
also drop tags deleted on the server
the honest alternative: a new version
